opening.headline: This addresses the issue of high input costs due to lengthy system prompts by discussing the conditions and effects of caching, which reuses a fixed prefix rather than re-entering it for each request.
body: The system prompt for customer service consists of 8,000 tokens comprising role instructions and policy rules, along with response examples. The user's query is only about 100 tokens. Each request results in processing all 8,000 tokens again, incurring the associated cost. If the service is called 100,000 times per day, it effectively processes the same content 100,000 times.

This lesson explains the principle of prompt caching—reusing the same prefix—and compares caching conditions across three companies. It then distinguishes between effective and ineffective cache designs, and calculates how much cost reduction occurs in services with long system prompts where only the question changes.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: This can explain the conditions under which prompt caching is effective and its effects.
It can distinguish between effective and ineffective cache designs and calculate the reduction scale.

screens.title: A long system prompt incurs costs for every request.
screens.lead: Consider the request configuration of the following service and think about where the costs are being incurred.

visual.alt: A diagram showing the repeated processing of the same system prompt for 8,000 tokens and a 100-token question for each request.

paragraphs: Customer support service is available. The system prompt includes role instructions, refund and exchange policy, and response examples, totaling 8,000 tokens. The average user query is 100 tokens. These numbers are based on assumptions for illustrative purposes.

Every time a request comes in, the model processes the full 8,100 tokens—comprising 8,000 tokens of system prompt and 100 tokens of question—from scratch, incurring input costs for the entire 8,100 tokens. If 100,000 requests come in per day, the same 8,000-token system prompt is processed 100,000 times. Ninety-nine percent of the input content is identical to that of previous requests.

Caching is the method of storing the results of processing unchanged portions and reusing them later. This reduces processing time and costs. This lesson covers the conditions under which caching is effective, its limitations, and how to calculate its benefits.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Just enabling caching will always reduce costs? It may not be effective depending on request composition or request intervals. We check those conditions during the class.

screens.outro: First, let's recall where repetitive inputs occur in my service.

screens.title: Recall recurring input weightings
screens.lead: When an item is selected, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Since you haven't entered or submitted an answer, take a moment to reflect on your request to my service first.

items.prompt: How long are system prompts and role instructions, and how frequently do they change?
items.answer: This is the first candidate for caching. If it is long and nearly unchanged, the effect will be significant. It's worth examining whether, even if it frequently changes, the changing portions can be moved to the end.

Tool definitions are fixed content attached to each request. In Claude, the cache prefix is constructed in the order of tool, system, and message, so tool definitions are placed at the very beginning as fixed content. OpenAI also includes tool definitions within the cached rendered context; however, if the tool name or order changes, the cache becomes inconsistent.

items.prompt: Fixed reference documentation or examples, what about the beginning of the longer conversation history?
items.answer: Reference documents with multiple examples and repeated queries are typical cache candidates. When conversations grow long, previous turns remain unchanged, so caching the earlier portion and only processing new turns thereafter is sufficient. Recognizing the prominence of recurring inputs should be the starting point of the design.

screens.outro: Let's verify how caching works by examining the actual request structure.

screens.title: The principle of prompt caching: reuse the prefix.
screens.lead: Prompt caching is a feature that reuses previously computed states when the prefix of a request matches that of a prior request. When the model processes input, it creates intermediate states used in subsequent computations; what is cached is not the tokens themselves, but these intermediate states. The following shows how the Claude request marks the end of its prefix. Please read the code and verify the explanation on the right.

notes.note: At the end of the system block, appending cache_control indicates that the portion up to here is cacheable. The content preceding this block and the block itself are subject to caching. If no such indication is present, caching does not occur. Furthermore, if any character within this block changes, the cache prior to that point becomes invalid and cannot be used.

This is a fixed content slot of 8,000 tokens. For a cache hit to occur, the entire text must be exactly the same across requests. If the current timestamp or user name is included within this text, the content will vary with each request, resulting in no cache hit.

The type of cache_control: ephemeral means a cache with a default lifetime of 5 minutes. The cache lifetime is renewed automatically each time the cached content is used, without additional cost. If no subsequent request arrives within 5 minutes, the cache expires and must be reprocessed and re-recorded.

Messages contain questions that vary with each request. Since they appear after the prefix, they are processed anew regardless of caching. Variable values should always be placed behind this section. There is also an automatic caching mechanism that follows the entire conversation history by setting cache_control once at the top level of the request.

screens.outro: Let's compare side by side the caching conditions and verification methods of the three companies.

To achieve a cache hit, instruct clients to send requests with similar prefixes within a short time frame.
After GPT-5.6, the default lifespan is 30 minutes, and a minimum lifespan of 12 hours can be selected via the Responses API.

The reduced amount is automatically transmitted upon successful match. No separate settings are required.

data.notes: All three services follow the same principle that prefixes must match starting from the front. Prefixes shorter than the minimum length are not cached and do not cause errors, so the number of cache hits must be verified. If both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens are zero in Claude, then no caching occurred.

screens.outro: Now that I know the conditions, I will compare designs that work with caching and those that do not.

screens.title: Cache-friendly design and cache-unfriendly design
screens.lead: When you alternately select two state buttons to design the same service in two different ways, compare how the cache behaves differently in each case.

states.label: Cache-friendly design
states.body: Place fixed content such as roles, rules, reference documents, and examples at the front of the prompt, and keep variable questions at the back. When a request comes in, the first 8,000 tokens remain exactly the same as previous requests and are served from cache, while only the last 100 tokens are processed anew. Gemini also recommends placing large documents and common content at the beginning of the prompt and sending similar prefixes shortly after each other. Stable matching is achieved when the prefix exceeds a minimum length and the request interval is longer than the lifespan.

states.label: Cache-incompatible design
states.body: If you insert variable values such as the current time or user name at the beginning of the system prompt, the prefix changes with each request, and caching is broken from that point onward, causing all 8,000 tokens after it to be reprocessed. Claude warns that in such cases, the system may only incur the cost of writing a new cache entry for each request, while reading from cache never occurs. If the prefix is shorter than the minimum length, it is not eligible for caching, and if the request interval exceeds its lifespan, the cache expires. Even if the order or settings of tool definitions change, the prefix becomes misaligned. Pay attention to the fact that the two designs contain identical content but differ only in order. The caching design does not involve adding new features, but rather reorganizing the existing prompt structure, making it a highly cost-effective and easily implementable optimization. After making such changes, you must always verify whether the actual number of read tokens has increased in the response usage field.

screens.outro: Based on this design principle, let's directly calculate the reduction scale.

screens.title: The principle of reducing lengthy system prompts in services where only the question changes
screens.lead: The instructor calculates the input cost for a service with 100,000 requests per day before and after caching. Select the arrows to proceed step by step and follow the calculation process.

steps.title: Assumption
steps.body: The fixed prefix is 8,000 tokens, the query is 100 tokens, and daily requests amount to 100,000. The model is assumed to be Sonnet 5.5, with an input cost of $2 per 1,000 tokens, cache write cost of $2.50, and cache read cost of $0.10. Response cost is independent of caching, so only input costs are compared.

steps.title: Step 1. When cache is not available
steps.body: Each request consumes a total of 8,100 tokens, all processed at the standard input rate. Daily input amounts to 8,100 × 100,000 = 810 million tokens, or 810 MTok. Multiplying this by $2 results in a daily input cost of $1,620.

steps.title: Step 2. Fix the prefix and when the cache is enabled
steps.body: 8,000 tokens are processed at cache read cost, and 100 tokens at regular cost. Read tokens amount to 8,000 × 100,000 = 800 MTok, multiplied by a unit price of $0.10, resulting in $80. Question tokens amount to 100 × 100,000 = 10 MTok, multiplied by $2, resulting in $20. Assuming the request does not terminate and the cache remains active, the recording cost is approximately 8,000 tokens × $2.50, amounting to just a few cents.

steps.title: Step 3. Cost Comparison
steps.body: Cache cost drops from $1,620 to approximately $100, representing a reduction of about 94%. Most of this reduction comes from the per-token cost decreasing from $2 to $0.10 for repeated sequences of 8,000 tokens. Processing time also decreases because it no longer needs to recalculate input. These figures are based on assumptions for illustrative purposes and should be recalculated using actual pricing and traffic data.

steps.title: Step 4. Verification: Are we truly hitting the mark?
steps.body: The calculation is based on the assumption that the cache hit. Verify whether the request interval is within the lifetime, whether the prefix is at least the minimum length, and whether variable values are mixed into the prefix. Then check whether the number of read tokens actually increased in the response's usage field. If the read token count is zero, the savings are also zero.

screens.outro: Summarize the key points at the final screen.

screens.title: Fixing a prefix incurs a cost.
screens.lead: This lesson's key points are summarized. Please review your answers to the questions posed in the problem presentation screen.

paragraphs: Caching is a function that stores and reuses the processing state of input prompts, not response data, and only the prefix matching portion is reused. Therefore, the design principle is to place fixed content at the front and variable values at the back.

Going back to the first question, enabling caching does not always reduce costs. There is no benefit when the minimum length is not met, the lifespan has expired, or variable values are mixed into the prefix. It is necessary to habitually verify the effectiveness by measuring the number of matching tokens in responses. Furthermore, the extent of cost reduction depends on the proportion of repeated inputs and request frequency. The savings are greater when the prefix is long and requests are frequent, and smaller when the prefix is short or requests are rare. Therefore, before redesigning, it is essential to first reassess the token count of fixed prefixes and request intervals.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The token count, request count, and price in the text are assumptions for illustrative purposes. Recalculate the pricing based on actual rates and traffic.

checks.intro: Pair up to check for cache hits. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Check how cache hit status is verified and pair it with the company.
right: Target rate monitoring on the dashboard
checks.explain: Since each company has a different location for checking cache hits, you should verify the response's usage field or dashboard.

checks.intro: Recall the two designs you just compared and verify them for yourself. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: We inserted the current time at the beginning of the system prompt, but cache hits dropped significantly. What could be the reason?
options: The timestamp increases the token count, causing the cache limit to be exceeded.
The prefix changes every time, causing the cache to break at that point.
Cache cannot store prompts containing time information.
The current time is a output-side value that conflicts with the input cache.
checks.explain: Cache is severed at the first character difference. Fixed content must come first, followed by variable values.

wrong.0: The problem is not the token count but the mismatch of prefixes.
wrong.2: Matching on prefixes is the condition, not whether it is storable.
wrong.3: Time is part of the input, and the issue is changing the prefix.

glossary.def: A feature that reuses the previously processed prompt prefix to reduce cost and delay.
This design places content that does not change per request at the very beginning of the prompt.
The minimum length that a prefix must have to become a cache target.
This is the duration for which cache is maintained. There is also a method that refreshes it each time it is used.

misconceptions.fact: What is stored is the processing state of the input prompt, and the response is regenerated each time.

misconceptions.myth: You don't need to match the prompt exactly—just getting halfway there is enough to hit the mark.
misconceptions.fact: Only a complete prefix match from the beginning is reused. If the prefix differs by even one character, the cache is broken at that point.
It is not beneficial if the token count is below the minimum or if the request interval exceeds the lifetime. The number of matched tokens must be verified.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Cache reuses only the matching portion starting from the front.
Incorporate minimum token and validity conditions into the design.
Verify the effectiveness by checking the number of matching response tokens.
